transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I suppose what brought me in is... I just keep getting up. Like, at staff meetings or even at dinner when everyone else is comfortably seated, I'll just suddenly need to go refill my coffee, or check a handout, or walk to the back of the room, even though nothing is really urgent at all. 

Speaking of coffee, they actually just switched the brand in the teachers' lounge at my school. It's some sort of dark roast now, and honestly, it is terribly bitter. I mentioned it to the principal—he's been there for, gosh, fifteen years, ever since my son was in middle school. My son is an architect now, by the way, living up in Chicago. It's so incredibly cold there, I visited him last Thanksgiving and nearly froze my ears off waiting for a taxi... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the meetings. Yes, I just keep leaving my chair when I'm supposed to be sitting down.
When you're sitting in these meetings, are you able to focus on what's being said, or do you find your mind wandering or having trouble concentrating?

Oh, no, I don't really have trouble focusing on what's being said. I hear everything just fine when I'm actually in the room. It's just that the things they talk about are so... well, repetitive. 

Like yesterday, they were going over the new district grading software again. It's this dreadful program, I think it's called Edu-Track? My colleague Brenda—she teaches AP Chemistry down the hall from me—she spent three hours trying to log in on Tuesday night. She actually called me at 8 PM to complain! I was right in the middle of making my chicken cacciatore. I use my grandmother's recipe, you know, and the secret is just a little splash of dry white wine right before you let it simmer. You wouldn't believe the difference it makes in the sauce, it really brightens the whole dish up. 

Anyway, Brenda was just furious about the passwords requiring all these special characters now. But, um... what did you ask me? Oh, right, concentrating. No, my mind doesn't really wander off like that, I just get this overwhelming urge to stand up and move around.

Outside of these meetings at school, do you find yourself having this same urge to get up and move around during other activities throughout your day—like when you're at home in the evening, or during meals, or other times when you're expected to stay seated?

Yes, exactly, like I was saying before about dinner! It happens all the time at home, too. When everyone else is perfectly happily seated at the table, I'll just pop up. I'll suddenly decide I need to go grab a different napkin, or get up to refill my water glass, or just walk into the kitchen to check if I left the porch light on, even though absolutely nothing is urgent. 

My husband gets so exasperated with me. We went out to this lovely little Italian place for our anniversary last month—Luigi's, over on 4th Street. Have you been? They make their own pasta from scratch right there in the window. I had the butternut squash ravioli, and oh my goodness, the sage butter sauce was just divine. I actually tried to recreate it at home last weekend, but I think I browned the butter a little too much. It's such a fine line, isn't it? Between perfectly nutty browned butter and just... burnt. I ended up having to throw the whole pan out and we just ordered a pizza instead. The delivery boy was so late, too, I think he got lost because our street sign is covered by that massive oak tree... 

Wait, what was the question again? Oh, right, moving around. Yes, dinners, evenings at home in the living room... I just keep getting up for no real reason when I'm supposed to be sitting down.

When you get that urge to stand up and move around, does it feel like there's a physical restlessness or fidgetiness in your body—like your legs or muscles feel uncomfortable if you stay still—or does it feel more like your mind is jumping to other things you need to do?

It's definitely more of a physical thing, yes. Like, if I'm sitting at my desk grading essays or when I'm in church, I always catch myself tapping my foot or clicking my pen. I shift around in my seat so much that I actually have to mentally remind myself to just settle down. 

Speaking of church, Pastor Thomas gave the most incredibly long sermon this past Sunday. It was about the virtue of patience, which is a bit ironic, I suppose! He's a lovely man, but he really does drone on. His wife, Mary, though—she makes the absolute best peach cobbler for the summer bake sale. I always make sure to buy two tins before they sell out. I actually tried growing my own peaches in the backyard a few years ago, but the squirrels got to every single one before they were even ripe. They are such absolute menaces! I even bought one of those special bird feeders that spins around to throw them off, but the squirrels just treated it like a carnival ride, holding on for dear life and spinning in circles... 

Oh, goodness, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Right, the restless feeling. Yes, I just get very fidgety and have to keep moving my feet or shifting my weight when I'm sitting still.

When did you first notice this restlessness and fidgeting—the urge to move around and difficulty staying still? Has this been something you've dealt with your whole life, or is it something that started more recently?

Oh, it's been my whole life, really. Even as a little girl, I remember my report cards always saying the same thing. They'd write that I was a bright student, but I just could not stay in my seat or wait my turn to speak. My mother used to joke that I wore a literal path in the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! 

Speaking of pencil sharpeners, do you remember those old metal ones they used to bolt to the walls in classrooms? The ones with the crank handle? They were so loud, but they gave you the absolute perfect point on a number two pencil. Now everything is mechanical or those cheap plastic handheld ones that just eat the lead. I buy the Ticonderoga ones for my classroom out of my own pocket because the district supplies these dreadful generic pencils that just snap the second you put any pressure on them. It's ridiculous how little funding we get for basic supplies. Last year, the PTA had to run a massive wrapping paper fundraiser just to buy copy paper. I ended up buying fifty dollars worth of wrapping paper myself, and I don't even wrap presents that often! I usually just use those decorative gift bags. You just pop some tissue paper in the top and it looks so elegant, plus you can reuse them. I have a whole closet full of them at home, organized by occasion... 

I'm sorry, I've done it again, haven't I? What was the question? Oh, right, how long it's been happening. Yes, since I was a child. I've always been this way.

No evidence of anxiety symptoms, worry, or tension. The tangential speech and difficulty staying on topic are characteristic of ADHD rather than GAD.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with lifelong history of physical restlessness, fidgeting, and difficulty remaining seated across multiple contexts (meetings, meals, church, home). She exhibits prominent motor restlessness with foot tapping, pen clicking, and constant shifting. Notably, she denies inattention and concentration difficulties—she explicitly states she 'hears everything just fine' and her mind doesn't 'wander off.' The symptom profile is predominantly hyperkinetic-impulsive type (F90.0 would be more specific), but given the absence of clear inattention criteria and the patient's tangential speech pattern (which may reflect her communication style rather than core ADHD inattention), F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) is most appropriate. The patient also demonstrates significant verbal tangentiality throughout the interview, which could suggest some attentional processing differences, but this appears more consistent with personality/communication style than core inattention symptoms.
